items.readable_text:
Content:
A rational function is defined for all values of [MATH: x] except for those at vertical asymptotes and holes. So, to find the domain, we must exclude all values of [MATH: x] that make the denominator zero.

Content:
For instance, suppose we want to define the domain of the rational function [MATH: f(x),] given by

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x^2-5x+6}.]

Content:
Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} − 5x + 6|= 0; (x − 2)(x − 3)|= 0; x|= 2, 3.]

Content:
Therefore, the domain is [MATH: x \in \left( -\infty, 2\right) \cup \left( 2,3 \right) \cup \left( 3,\infty \right),] as we can see in the graph of the function below.

Graphic:

items.readable_text:
Content:
Finding the range of a rational function is not as straightforward as finding the domain. Here, we will focus on finding the range of a rational function in the simple case when the numerator and denominator are linear expressions.

Content:
One way to find the range of such a rational function [MATH: f(x)] is to find the domain of its inverse function [MATH: f^{-1}(x).]

Content:
To illustrate, let's find the range of the function [MATH: f(x),] given by

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x}{x-2}.]

Content:
First, we set [MATH: y = f(x)] and make [MATH: x] the subject of the equation, as follows:

Content:
[MATH: y|= (x)/(x − 2); y(x − 2)|= x; xy − 2y|= x; xy − x|= 2y; x(y − 1)|= 2y; x|= (2y)/(y − 1)]

Content:
The above equation tells us that the right-hand side exists for all values of [MATH: y] except for those that make the denominator zero.

Content:
Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

Content:
[MATH: y − 1|= 0; y|= 1.]

Content:
Therefore, the range is [MATH: f(x) \in \left( -\infty, 1\right) \cup \left( 1,\infty \right),] as we can see in the graph of the function below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/29819c5786465b27e6470786ce4c646e]

sections.normalized_html: What is the range of the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x-5}{2x-5}?]
sections.readable_text: What is the range of the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x-5}{2x-5}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
One way to determine the range of a rational function [MATH: f(x)] is to find the domain of its inverse function [MATH: f^{-1}(x).]

First, let's set [MATH: y = f(x)] and make [MATH: x] the subject of the equation, as follows:

[MATH: y|= (x − 5)/(2x − 5); y(2x − 5)|= x − 5; 2xy − 5y|= x − 5; 2xy − x|= 5y − 5; x(2y − 1)|= 5y − 5; x|= (5y − 5)/(2y − 1)]

The above equation tells us that the right-hand side exists for all values of [MATH: y] except for those that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

[MATH: 2y − 1|= 0; 2y|= 1; y|= (1)/(2).]

Therefore, the range is [MATH: f(x) \in \left( -\infty, \dfrac1 2\right) \cup \left( \dfrac1 2,\infty \right).]

items.title: Finding the Range of a Rational Function Containing Holes

sections.normalized_html: What is the range of the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x-1}{3x^2-2x-1}?]
sections.readable_text: What is the range of the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x-1}{3x^2-2x-1}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's factor the numerator and denominator: [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x-1}{3x^2-2x-1} = \dfrac{x-1}{(3x+1)(x-1)}]

Notice that the numerator and denominator both have [MATH: (x-1)] as a common factor. Setting this common factor equal to zero and solving for [MATH: x] gives

[MATH: x - 1 = 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x= 1.]

Therefore, the function has a hole at [MATH: x = 1.]

To find the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole, we find the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x)] and evaluate it at the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the hole.

Finding the reduced rational function [MATH: F(x),] we get

[MATH: F(x)|= (x − 1)/((3x + 1)(x − 1)); = (x − 1)/((3x + 1)(x − 1)); = (1)/(3x + 1).]

The [MATH: y]-coordinate of the hole is given by [MATH: F(1)|= (1)/(3(1) + 1); = (1)/(4).]

So, the coordinates of the hole are [MATH: \left(1, \dfrac14\right).]

Now, let's make [MATH: x] the subject of the simplified equation, as follows:

[MATH: y|= (1)/(3x + 1); y(3x + 1)|= 1; 3xy + y|= 1; 3xy|= 1 − y; x|= (1 − y)/(3y)]

The above equation tells us that the right-hand side exists for all values of [MATH: y] except for those that make the denominator zero.

Setting the denominator equal to zero and solving, we get

[MATH: 3y = 0⟹y = 0.]

Therefore, the range is [MATH: f(x) \in \left( -\infty, 0\right) \cup \left( 0,\dfrac1 4 \right) \cup \left( \dfrac 1 4,\infty \right).]
